PORTS IN PERIL

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
ARE TRANSNET PORTS HOLDING THE ECONOMY TO RANSOM AS DELAYS MEAN SHIPS BYPASS OUR PORTS

Unique Selling Point:
Interview with Transnet and visuals on the Terminal that one normally has no access to

Summary:
As deterioration of our ports reaches mission critical, shippers, truckers, importers and exporters are tearing their hair out with substantial delays that are costing their businesses, the economy and our international reputation, millions in lost revenue.

80- 90% of our economy relies on our ports, but by July this year after five years of dismal performance by Transnet Ports Terminals, shippers, truckers, citrus growers and freight forwarders had had enough, and wrote a letter to President Ramaphosa. In it, they implored the president to intervene and help find solutions fast, or the economy would contract further and there would be more job losses. Transnet literally holds the fate of the economy in its hands.



Further information:
DURBAN
The Durban container terminal is probably the worst. Here ships can wait up to two weeks outside the port for a birth. At 30 000 USD per day per ship, the costs borne by the shipping lines are enormous, and they too have had enough. For the last five years they have been sounding warnings to Transnet but things have got worse not better. But these delays have had consequences – ships are starting to bypass our shores so they can make the slots they have booked in Europe and that has been diabolical for South Africa’s export industry.

ROTTING FRUIT
Mitchell Brooke represents the Citrus Growers association. They represent one of South Africa’s biggest export markets, that is projected to grow by 25%. But if the ports continue in the same vein, that entire industry could collapse. It was Mitchell’s idea to write the desperate plea to the president.

PORT ELIZABETH
Two of the biggest citrus exporters Paul Marais and Mark Jenson have been through the worst ever season in July. In Port Elizabeth containers sat on the port for almost a month as one ship after another passed by – by the time their fruit arrived in Moscow and Canada it was rejected. Its cost them hundreds of millions of rand, and our reputation as reliable suppliers is now in ICU. If the situation is not fixed by next season we might as well say goodbye to one of our best earners of foreign exchange.

A FURIOUS CEO
At Volkswagen in Uitenhage the CEO Thomas Schaefer is mad as a snake and when Transnet came to see him, he gave them hell. Hardly surprising, Volkwagen imports certain parts and thanks to the inefficiency at the ports his usual 400 units per day went down to 80.

LOSING THE EDGE TO AFRICAN PORTS
In the letter to the president comparisons are made between the time it takes to load a container on our ships in our ports versus those in Africa. We are only marginally better than Mogadishu which has been at war, and many others are far more productive than ours. Small wonder that ships are bypassing our ports and using Maputo or Walvis Bay where the Chinese have invested heavily. So long Durban, PE and Cape Town. Data shows that ships arriving at our ports are down by 20%.


MILITANT WORKERS AND LOW PRODUCTIVITY
For transporter Philip Darne in PE, he says the tail is wagging the dog. Workers rule the roost and if they don’t feel like working, they simply don’t. He says some managers are trying but he thinks they get worn down. Last year a crane blew into the Harbour in PE and it’s still there. He has a fleet of 50 trucks but he is thinking of closing up shop and emigrating. It’s got so bad he says that the trucking companies coming in to Port to load and offload containers are actually subsiding the operations and are working at huge losses.

The data supports his contention. In Shanghai a shift change for crane drivers takes two minutes. In Transnet’s ports it can take up to one and a half hours. And that is just one small example. In Durban the low productivity of the workers translates to queues to trucks at times up to 10 kilometers long, waiting to enter port to pick up or drop off containers. Drivers can sit for anything up to 18 hours to get into port when the target turnaround time according to Transnet is 45 minutes. It’s no longer worth it for many as they find themselves on the wrong end of the time is money principle. Others have been forced to close down.

DECAYING EQUIPMENT
Mitchell Brooke decided to go and see for himself and took himself on a tour last month of the maintenance bays and the gear we rely on to make our ports work. It was a shocking experience he tells Carte Blanche and far worse than he ever imagined. He found oil leaking from cranes, safety issues, and equipment that is old and broken.

Kevin Martin has been in the industry for years and is well known amongst many of those that rely on the ports. Kevin has done an audit on what we have and what we need and a conversation with him leaves one in no doubt that we are in serious trouble. If we want to get into detail, he can tell us how many straddles we need and how many we are short down to every crane and nut and bolt!


THE GOOD NEWS: TRANSNET IS TRYING  To be fair to Transnet – Cyril sent the letter to Pravin and Pravin listened to the problem. And we thought he had his hands full with Eskom and the EFF and the public protector! It wasn’t long before Popo Molefe Chairman of Transnet, responded and promised immediate action. The new CEO, of our worst port Michelle Phillips also sent a detailed letter with action plans and target to the CEO of the Citrus Growers association.

THE BAD NEWS: THEY’RE NOT TRYING HARD ENOUGH
But despite their best intentions Transnet has already missed some of its self-imposed deadlines and ask around to those who regularly use the ports and they say nothing has improved.





AND TRANSNET IS IN THE POO
Transnet, itself still recovering from years of state Capture have just released their financials. They make for grim reading. Over R40 billion rand in irregular expenditure and unable to pay their debts – so where will the money come from for their much needed infrastructure upgrade

Ports in Peril FINAL SCRIPT

Commentary One
On any given day, trucks begin to line up on Bayhead road in Durban- there to collect or drop off containers at Transnet’s Container Terminal for export. A round trip used to take them 90 minutes.

Up sound truck

But not anymore, delays are killing the transport business says Sue Moodley, chairperson of the Harbour carriers association

Derek
Give us an idea of the delays?
Sue Moodley
The trucks could stand in there for six hours on a good day, 12 hours, 15 hours, 18 hours, 24 hours and sometimes even 36 hours!

DEREK LINK
It’s all about the boxes, getting these containers off the ships and out of the harbor as quickly as possible, but that is where things can go horribly wrong

Commentary two
And at almost every one of our ports, it has. Low productivity has meant ships languish out at sea for days, waiting for a berth in the port, while trucks idle for hours and their drivers just wait – with no access to ablutions.

Sue Moodley
On a good day if you have to stand in the terminal and say you are waiting for 6 hours or ten hours, you are looking at about R5 million and on a bad day, it can go up to R10 million- so it’s a huge loss to the economy

Commentary three
And the losses for the shipping lines are even bigger. Captain Sarno, chairman of MSC estimates they have three ships per day in our ports, and each vessel is delayed by an average of three days

Captain Sarno
The cost is 30 000 US per day/ we have lost something like 10 million dollars
Derek
10 million dollars?
Sarno
I mean that is unbelievable!
Derek
In what period?
Captain Sarno
In six months!

Commentary Four
He has diagnosed exactly what is wrong with the ports and it starts, he says with leadership.

Captain Sarno
Today we have an acting CE of the terminal, an acting Group CO, an acting operations managers. They are all acting and the result is no one is doing anything!

Commentary Five
Even the basics -spares like tyres and oil weren’t available for these straddle carriers that move containers around, so many lay broken outside the maintenance bays. And for years, the captain says he has been asking for more skilled workers- called gangs, by the industry.

Captain Sarno
Because even if now these fourteen gangs come there are not enough straddle carriers. So they have no machinery!

Commentary Six
Peter Besnard represents around 104 shipping lines and agents. By midyear they were so desperate, they wrote to President Ramaphosa asking for urgent intervention at our ports

Derek
Peter why did you take this extreme step of communicating with the president?
Peter Besnard
Every meeting we went to we were shown projections of what they were going to do and how they were going to do it but we never got any further

Commentary Seven
Now the shipping lines are considering a 500 USD surcharge on every container they deliver

CAPTAIN SARNO
I warn the people in charge, president Ramaphosa, to pay attention because if not done, something, something now. Yesterday not tomorrow! This implementation of the congestion surcharge will be on hey!

Commentary eight
But the president may be listening , and in August Michelle Phillips, who has spent years at senior level in the ports, became the Acting chief executive

Derek
Michelle, from the research we have done you have a massive hurdle to jump
Michelle
Yes and it’s not an impossible hurdle.
Derek
Now looking at it Michelle what is it. Is it infrastructure, equipment, inefficient port workers, pathetic management, bad maintenance?
Michelle
It is a mixture of a number of factors, when you think you have cleared up one- another happens -What is important is that we keep our eye on the total picture and we try to pull these levers in the best possible way to ensure we get out of the situation we are in

Commentary nine
As part of their recovery, Phillips needs to urgently increase productivity. This is measured by the industry on how many container moves we make, per crane per hour- The more you do, the faster the ships can leave again.

Up sound

Other ports average around 24 moves per hour. Durban once managed that easily. Not anymore, down now to a sad 17. Cape Town does around 18, and the port at Coega- a miserable 14. Even Mogadishu’s port does better than that.

Derek
Rate the current performance of the ports out of ten
Michelle
Five
Derek
Five you are giving yourself five? Isn’t that pushing it?
Michelle
Not pushing it. I think we are having a situation we need to get out of it,maybe come see me in 18 months and we will be a ten!

Commentary ten
But speak to the trucking companies that deliver and collect containers from the ports and their ratings are less generous.

Derek
How would you rate their efficiency on a scale of 1- 10?
Philip
Can we go to minus?
Derek
That bad?
Philip
Terrible!

Commentary eleven
Philip Darne says his trucking company is battling to survive. Delays in Coega and Port Elizabeth push overtime costs through the roof. His company services the motor industry and that too has been affected by Transnet delays

Derek
In your opinion who runs the port?
Philip
The staff, the laborers, definitely not management
Derek
Not management
Philip
No management need to get a handle on it.

Up sound from video of truck lines into Ngqura

In June, even before port workers went on a go slow, this was the queue into the port at Coega.

Up sound 8,9, 10, eleven I am not even going to count there are so many trucks

Derek
The concern here Michelle is that the tail is wagging the dog, the workers run the ports?
Michelle
I firmly believe that once people have what they need to be productive, it then enables myself as well as the leadership below me to manage performance in the way it should be managed.

Commentary twelve
Transnet says it has an appointment system to avoid congestion and the trucks aren’t using it. The truckers say they don’t make their appointments because they can’t get into the ports due to congestion - and they don’t agree with the way the delays are measured by Transnet

Philip
The time that they measure is from the time that they let it in. All the vehicles are behind in the queue but they measure from the time that it goes in the gate. So the trucks are spending five hours outside the gate but they only measure from the time they let it in.

LINK
The delays are having a knock- on effect across the board – shipping companies can’t afford to have their vessels out at sea for days on end so they simply bypass our ports and that is having a catastrophic effect on our imports and exports

Commentary thirteen
Down in the Sunday’s river valley, citrus is the life blood of the Eastern Cape, but this year Transnet almost strangled it to death. Paul Marais is the chairman of Sundays River Citrus Company, a company owned by about 90 growers

Paul Marais
Its company ending stuff! if you are growing citrus but you can’t get your produce overseas, it ends that business.

Commentary fourteen
This season they had signed contracts across the world from Russia to Canada to Sainsbury’s in the UK

Paul
and normally what would happen is that the container would be loaded and shipped within a week, 5- 7 days and this year the wheels completely fell off. We had containers standing at the harbor for more than a month at a time

Commentary fifteen
While the citrus waited at the port, workers at Coega unhappy about a reduced performance bonus, went on a go slow. That meant congestion at Coega, but Port Elizabeth couldn’t cope either. It had only one working crane, the other lay in a crumpled heap after blowing over last year, so Transnet sent a replacement from Durban

Derek
Paul you are describing a perfect storm almost, what really went wrong?
Paul
I think positions filled with incompetent people. I don’t know how else to describe it – how do you bring a broken crane to replace a broken crane but the crane that you bring is broken? Its incompetence

Commentary Sixteen
The result was that ships skipped the ports to avoid costly delays, the fruit sat in refrigeration containers at the harbour at unsuitable temperatures and Canadian customers had empty shelves for most of July. Fruit exporter Mark Jensen

Mark Jensen
We had programmes that were for 23 containers per week for a retailer, arriving from beginning of July on a weekly basis till the end of July- as a result of delays, congestion, vessels skipping the ports all 92 of those containers arrived simultaneously in the last week of July.

Derek
Can you quantify the losses financially?
Paul Marais
I don’t have the exact number right now but what I can tell you is that in this valley it amounts to hundreds of millions of rands. If you think this valley exports twenty million cartons and if we only destroyed ten rand per carton value, that is R200 million rand just off the top of my head. It’s just gone you can never recover it gone! it’s done!

Commentary seventeen
The citrus growers association which represents this R20 billion industry implored Minister Pravin Gordhan to intervene and things have begun to improve says CEO Justin Chadwick

Justin Chadwick
From Transnet side the acting CE has kept us abreast in terms of their action plan and in terms of the workforce it seems they are getting things in place, where we are still worried about is the equipment

Derek
Are you confident that you can do it?
Michelle
I am a firm believer. I have been in this business Derek for 20 years. In fact this is not the worst we have seen. What I am going to say is that it requires patience, it requires commitment…
Derek
How much patience when it’s costing millions per day?
Michelle
It requires a bit of patience, it requires extreme commitment from all parties, and everybody in this system needs to own their responsibility and do what need to be done so that we can grow not just Transnet, the country

Derek to Paul
They say they have an action plan?
Paul Marais
Paul laughs. I have heard they have an action plan you know talk is cheap, money buys whisky isn’t it…just get back to basics and our private sector will grow the economy

THE END 12 06.

PROMO ONE
Shipping lines, truckers. Exporters and importers are up in arms about the costly delays at
at our ports
Paul Marais
You can’t get your produce overseas it ends that business

PROMO TWO
Crippling delays at our ports have left the shipping industry fuming.
Captain Sarno
we have lost something like 10 million dollars!
Derek
10 million dollars?

PROMO THREE
With severe delays at our ports, shipping lines, truckers and exporters have lost patience. Now new boss Michelle Phillips is facing the challenge of her career to turn things around.

Michelle It is a mixture of a number of factors, when you think you have cleared up one- another happens -What is important is that we keep our eye on the total picture and we try to pull these levers in the best possible way to ensure we get out of the situation we are in Commentary nine As part of their recovery, Phillips needs to urgently increase productivity. This is measured by the industry on how many container moves we make, per crane per hour- The more you do, the faster the ships can leave again. Up sound Other ports average around 24 moves per hour. Durban once managed that easily. Not anymore, down now to a sad 17. Cape Town does around 18, and the port at Coega- a miserable 14. Even Mogadishu’s port does better than that. Derek Rate the current performance of the ports out of ten Michelle Five Derek Five you are giving yourself five? Isn’t that pushing it? Michelle Not pushing it. I think we are having a situation we need to get out of it,maybe come see me in 18 months and we will be a ten! Commentary ten But speak to the trucking companies that deliver and collect containers from the ports and their ratings are less generous. Derek How would you rate their efficiency on a scale of 1- 10? Philip Can we go to minus? Derek That bad? Philip Terrible! Commentary eleven Philip Darne says his trucking company is battling to survive. Delays in Coega and Port Elizabeth push overtime costs through the roof. His company services the motor industry and that too has been affected by Transnet delays Derek In your opinion who runs the port? Philip The staff, the laborers, definitely not management Derek Not management Philip No management need to get a handle on it. Up sound from video of truck lines into Ngqura In June, even before port workers went on a go slow, this was the queue into the port at Coega. Up sound 8,9, 10, eleven I am not even going to count there are so many trucks Derek The concern here Michelle is that the tail is wagging the dog, the workers run the ports? Michelle I firmly believe that once people have what they need to be productive, it then enables myself as well as the leadership below me to manage performance in the way it should be managed. Commentary twelve Transnet says it has an appointment system to avoid congestion and the trucks aren’t using it. The truckers say they don’t make their appointments because they can’t get into the ports due to congestion - and they don’t agree with the way the delays are measured by Transnet Philip The time that they measure is from the time that they let it in. All the vehicles are behind in the queue but they measure from the time that it goes in the gate. So the trucks are spending five hours outside the gate but they only measure from the time they let it in. LINK The delays are having a knock- on effect across the board – shipping companies can’t afford to have their vessels out at sea for days on end so they simply bypass our ports and that is having a catastrophic effect on our imports and exports Commentary thirteen Down in the Sunday’s river valley, citrus is the life blood of the Eastern Cape, but this year Transnet almost strangled it to death. Paul Marais is the chairman of Sundays River Citrus Company, a company owned by about 90 growers Paul Marais Its company ending stuff! if you are growing citrus but you can’t get your produce overseas, it ends that business. Commentary fourteen This season they had signed contracts across the world from Russia to Canada to Sainsbury’s in the UK Paul and normally what would happen is that the container would be loaded and shipped within a week, 5- 7 days and this year the wheels completely fell off. We had containers standing at the harbor for more than a month at a time Commentary fifteen While the citrus waited at the port, workers at Coega unhappy about a reduced performance bonus, went on a go slow. That meant congestion at Coega, but Port Elizabeth couldn’t cope either. It had only one working crane, the other lay in a crumpled heap after blowing over last year, so Transnet sent a replacement from Durban Derek Paul you are describing a perfect storm almost, what really went wrong? Paul I think positions filled with incompetent people. I don’t know how else to describe it – how do you bring a broken crane to replace a broken crane but the crane that you bring is broken? Its incompetence Commentary Sixteen The result was that ships skipped the ports to avoid costly delays, the fruit sat in refrigeration containers at the harbour at unsuitable temperatures and Canadian customers had empty shelves for most of July. Fruit exporter Mark Jensen Mark Jensen We had programmes that were for 23 containers per week for a retailer, arriving from beginning of July on a weekly basis till the end of July- as a result of delays, congestion, vessels skipping the ports all 92 of those containers arrived simultaneously in the last week of July. Derek Can you quantify the losses financially? Paul Marais I don’t have the exact number right now but what I can tell you is that in this valley it amounts to hundreds of millions of rands. If you think this valley exports twenty million cartons and if we only destroyed ten rand per carton value, that is R200 million rand just off the top of my head. It’s just gone you can never recover it gone! it’s done! Commentary seventeen The citrus growers association which represents this R20 billion industry implored Minister Pravin Gordhan to intervene and things have begun to improve says CEO Justin Chadwick Justin Chadwick From Transnet side the acting CE has kept us abreast in terms of their action plan and in terms of the workforce it seems they are getting things in place, where we are still worried about is the equipment Derek Are you confident that you can do it? Michelle I am a firm believer. I have been in this business Derek for 20 years. In fact this is not the worst we have seen. What I am going to say is that it requires patience, it requires commitment… Derek How much patience when it’s costing millions per day? Michelle It requires a bit of patience, it requires extreme commitment from all parties, and everybody in this system needs to own their responsibility and do what need to be done so that we can grow not just Transnet, the country Derek to Paul They say they have an action plan? Paul Marais Paul laughs. I have heard they have an action plan you know talk is cheap, money buys whisky isn’t it…just get back to basics and our private sector will grow the economy THE END 12 06. PROMO ONE Shipping lines, truckers. Exporters and importers are up in arms about the costly delays at at our ports Paul Marais You can’t get your produce overseas it ends that business PROMO TWO Crippling delays at our ports have left the shipping industry fuming. Captain Sarno we have lost something like 10 million dollars! Derek 10 million dollars? PROMO THREE With severe delays at our ports, shipping lines, truckers and exporters have lost patience. Now new boss Michelle Phillips is facing the challenge of her career to turn things around. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ARE TRANSNET PORTS HOLDING THE ECONOMY TO RANSOM AS DELAYS MEAN SHIPS BYPASS OUR PORTS
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Interview with Transnet and visuals on the Terminal that one normally has no access to
metadata.Summary: As deterioration of our ports reaches mission critical, shippers, truckers, importers and exporters are tearing their hair out with substantial delays that are costing their businesses, the economy and our international reputation, millions in lost revenue. 80- 90% of our economy relies on our ports, but by July this year after five years of dismal performance by Transnet Ports Terminals, shippers, truckers, citrus growers and freight forwarders had had enough, and wrote a letter to President Ramaphosa. In it, they implored the president to intervene and help find solutions fast, or the economy would contract further and there would be more job losses. Transnet literally holds the fate of the economy in its hands.
metadata.Further information: DURBAN The Durban container terminal is probably the worst. Here ships can wait up to two weeks outside the port for a birth. At 30 000 USD per day per ship, the costs borne by the shipping lines are enormous, and they too have had enough. For the last five years they have been sounding warnings to Transnet but things have got worse not better. But these delays have had consequences – ships are starting to bypass our shores so they can make the slots they have booked in Europe and that has been diabolical for South Africa’s export industry. ROTTING FRUIT Mitchell Brooke represents the Citrus Growers association. They represent one of South Africa’s biggest export markets, that is projected to grow by 25%. But if the ports continue in the same vein, that entire industry could collapse. It was Mitchell’s idea to write the desperate plea to the president. PORT ELIZABETH Two of the biggest citrus exporters Paul Marais and Mark Jenson have been through the worst ever season in July. In Port Elizabeth containers sat on the port for almost a month as one ship after another passed by – by the time their fruit arrived in Moscow and Canada it was rejected. Its cost them hundreds of millions of rand, and our reputation as reliable suppliers is now in ICU. If the situation is not fixed by next season we might as well say goodbye to one of our best earners of foreign exchange. A FURIOUS CEO At Volkswagen in Uitenhage the CEO Thomas Schaefer is mad as a snake and when Transnet came to see him, he gave them hell. Hardly surprising, Volkwagen imports certain parts and thanks to the inefficiency at the ports his usual 400 units per day went down to 80. LOSING THE EDGE TO AFRICAN PORTS In the letter to the president comparisons are made between the time it takes to load a container on our ships in our ports versus those in Africa. We are only marginally better than Mogadishu which has been at war, and many others are far more productive than ours. Small wonder that ships are bypassing our ports and using Maputo or Walvis Bay where the Chinese have invested heavily. So long Durban, PE and Cape Town. Data shows that ships arriving at our ports are down by 20%. MILITANT WORKERS AND LOW PRODUCTIVITY For transporter Philip Darne in PE, he says the tail is wagging the dog. Workers rule the roost and if they don’t feel like working, they simply don’t. He says some managers are trying but he thinks they get worn down. Last year a crane blew into the Harbour in PE and it’s still there. He has a fleet of 50 trucks but he is thinking of closing up shop and emigrating. It’s got so bad he says that the trucking companies coming in to Port to load and offload containers are actually subsiding the operations and are working at huge losses. The data supports his contention. In Shanghai a shift change for crane drivers takes two minutes. In Transnet’s ports it can take up to one and a half hours. And that is just one small example. In Durban the low productivity of the workers translates to queues to trucks at times up to 10 kilometers long, waiting to enter port to pick up or drop off containers. Drivers can sit for anything up to 18 hours to get into port when the target turnaround time according to Transnet is 45 minutes. It’s no longer worth it for many as they find themselves on the wrong end of the time is money principle. Others have been forced to close down. DECAYING EQUIPMENT Mitchell Brooke decided to go and see for himself and took himself on a tour last month of the maintenance bays and the gear we rely on to make our ports work. It was a shocking experience he tells Carte Blanche and far worse than he ever imagined. He found oil leaking from cranes, safety issues, and equipment that is old and broken. Kevin Martin has been in the industry for years and is well known amongst many of those that rely on the ports. Kevin has done an audit on what we have and what we need and a conversation with him leaves one in no doubt that we are in serious trouble. If we want to get into detail, he can tell us how many straddles we need and how many we are short down to every crane and nut and bolt! THE GOOD NEWS: TRANSNET IS TRYING To be fair to Transnet – Cyril sent the letter to Pravin and Pravin listened to the problem. And we thought he had his hands full with Eskom and the EFF and the public protector! It wasn’t long before Popo Molefe Chairman of Transnet, responded and promised immediate action. The new CEO, of our worst port Michelle Phillips also sent a detailed letter with action plans and target to the CEO of the Citrus Growers association. THE BAD NEWS: THEY’RE NOT TRYING HARD ENOUGH But despite their best intentions Transnet has already missed some of its self-imposed deadlines and ask around to those who regularly use the ports and they say nothing has improved. AND TRANSNET IS IN THE POO Transnet, itself still recovering from years of state Capture have just released their financials. They make for grim reading. Over R40 billion rand in irregular expenditure and unable to pay their debts – so where will the money come from for their much needed infrastructure upgrade
